name: Country-western dance

narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

instructor.persona: A knowledgeable social dance historian with a focus on regional American styles.
instructor.rule: counts out loud; demonstrates front and back; three slow repetitions before tempo; one correction at a time

This is Country-western dance. 18th century to present.

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The tradition originates from British and European dances like the Virginia Reel and quadrilles, adapted by American settlers.
Early 19th-century junkets and heel-burners are casual, all-night affairs.
African musical traditions, such as patting juba and the use of the banjo, provide the foundation for early American dance rhythms.
on_screen: Map: United States · North America

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Historically, dances accompany communal work events called frolics, serving as essential social gatherings for isolated frontier communities.
Today, they remain social activities held in clubs, dance halls, and community centers.
This is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: Let's Bootscoot 2 (https://archive.org/details/letsbootscoot2)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dances are categorized into couple, group, and line formations.
Couple dancing relies on a lead-and-follow dynamic where the man sets the pace.
The movement features a flat-footed glide.
Watch for the Cowboy Waltz.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is primarily country-western, drawing elements from pop and bluegrass.
Fiddles and banjos are historically central.
Listen for the fiddle, banjo, cotton hoe, and comb.
The music features fiddle-led melodies with rhythmic elements like patting juba and percussive sounds from improvised instruments.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: The style relies on cowboy boots, which dictate the gliding, flat-footed movement.
Historically, dances take place in large farmhouses, kitchens, town halls, or at ranch-based events.
Modern venues range from small lounges to massive nightclubs like the former Gilley's Club.
on_screen: Image gallery: 3 licensed images with attribution
Reconstruction imagery allowed only from the costume notes, labelled 'reconstruction'

scenes.title: The people
narration: Skippy Blair notes the popularity of country dance in a 1994 observation.
Music historian Bill C. Malone describes the early, mingled styles as a dance without a name.
Texas is known for kicker dancing, and West Texas ranch dances function as large-scale community events.
The tradition descends from European reels, quadrilles, and cotillions, transformed by American frontier culture and African-American musical influences.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Country-western dance is a variant of square dance, which develops from quadrilles and cotillions.
Country-western dance is a variant of clogging, an Appalachian step dance associated with bluegrass.
